alignment.note: Greek διεγερθείς ('having been awoken') is a passive participle implying Jesus was roused from sleep; the Vulgate exsurgens ('rising up') and the Peshitta ܘܩܡ ('and he arose', root q-w-m) both render the act as simple rising, losing the nuance of awakening from sleep present in the Greek. The Syriac ܘܩܡ is moreover bound to the preceding conjunction and serves a single finite verb where Greek employs a participle.

Greek ἐπετίμησεν is a single aorist finite verb 'he rebuked'; Latin renders it with the periphrastic perfect comminatus est (deponent), while Syriac ܘܟܐܐ (root k-a, 'to rebuke') is again coordinated with the conjunction. The constructions are semantically equivalent.

Greek uses the dative article + noun τῷ ἀνέμῳ and Latin the bare dative vento; the Peshitta ܒܪܘܚܐ marks the object of rebuke with the preposition ܒ ('against the wind'), a typical Syriac complementation of verbs of rebuking, whereas Greek and Latin govern a plain dative.

Greek πεφίμωσο is a perfect passive imperative ('be muzzled and stay so'), conveying a state to be entered and maintained; the Vulgate obmutesce is a present imperative and the Peshitta renders it analytically as ܙܓܝܪ ܐܢܬ ('you are silenced/restrained', passive participle + enclitic pronoun), reproducing the stative force of the Greek perfect through a periphrastic construction.
The high point after θαλάσσῃ and the Latin colon mark the transition to direct speech; punctuation only.

Greek ἐκόπασεν (κοπάζω, 'grew weary/abated') and Latin cessavit ('ceased') describe the wind's subsiding with active verbs; the Peshitta ܘܫܠܝܬ (root sh-l-y, 'became calm/still') reuses the same root just employed for the command ܫܠܝ, creating a deliberate lexical echo between Jesus' word to the sea and the wind's obedience that is absent in Greek and Latin.
The Latin colon after ventus parallels the Greek comma, marking clause division; punctuation only.

Greek γαλήνη and Latin tranquillitas both denote 'calm/stillness' of the sea; the Peshitta ܢܘܚܐ (root n-w-kh, 'rest, repose') is the cognate of the verb 'to rest', selecting a notion of restful quiet rather than the specifically nautical calm of the Greek term, though the semantic overlap is broad.
